content:
In this part of Numbers chapter fifteen, Yahweh deals with what happened when His commandments were broken unintentionally. If the whole congregation failed to observe something God had commanded through Moses, and the matter had been done unknowingly, then when the error at last became known, the congregation was not simply to ignore it because it had been accidental. They were to come before Yahweh according to the provision He had graciously made for them. The congregation was to present a young bull as a burnt offering, together with its grain offering and its drink offering, and a male goat as a sin offering. The priest would then make atonement for the whole congregation, and God said, "It shall be forgiven them, for it was unintentional" (Numbers 15:25). This provision even reached the foreigner living among them, so that no one who sincerely belonged to the people of God was left without a way back.

The same principle applied to a single individual who sinned unintentionally. That person was to bring a one-year-old female goat as a sin offering, the priest would make atonement before Yahweh, and the person would be forgiven (Numbers 15:27-29). So God made a clear distinction between something done unknowingly and deliberate rebellion against His Word. Sin that was committed in ignorance, once it was discovered, was not to be brushed aside as though it did not matter. It still required a sacrifice and atonement. But God, in His mercy, provided a way for it to be covered and forgiven. Ignorance did not make the sin nothing, but neither did it place the sinner beyond the reach of grace.

We have a later example in Scripture that shows what could happen when the people as a whole had greatly neglected the worship God had appointed. During the reign of King Hezekiah, the nation had been living in serious spiritual neglect. Hezekiah said that their fathers had been unfaithful, had turned their faces away from Yahweh's dwelling place, had shut the doors of the Temple, put out the lamps, and had stopped burning incense and presenting burnt offerings in the sanctuary (2 Chronicles 29:6-7).

So, he reopened the Temple, gathered the priests and Levites, and commanded that the sanctuary be cleansed. After the Temple had been purified, sacrifices were offered for all Israel, and the priests made atonement for the nation(2 Chronicles 29:20-24). Later, when the Passover was kept, many of the people had not properly purified themselves in the prescribed manner. Hezekiah interceded for them, asking God to pardon everyone whose heart was sincerely seeking Him, and Yahweh heard Hezekiah and healed the people(2 Chronicles 30:18-20).

We should be careful here, and note that the book of Chronicles does not specifically say that Israel was carrying out the exact law of Numbers 15:22-26. Nevertheless, if the nation had forgotten God's sanctuary, closed its doors, stopped its sacrifices, and neglected His commanded worship, then all the requirements God had given, including the instructions surrounding these offerings, had necessarily been neglected as part of that wider unfaithfulness. And so, their restoration involved exactly the same pattern: cleansing the sanctuary, returning to Yahweh, restoring His appointed worship, offering the sacrifices, receiving priestly atonement, praying, and receiving God's mercy.

It is a beautiful picture of how a people who had drifted far from God in ignorance and neglect could still be brought back when their hearts turned again to seek Him.

But then Numbers 15:30-31 makes a very serious distinction. Yahweh turns from the person who sins unintentionally to the person who sins defiantly, or as the Scripture says, "with a high hand." This is not someone who forgot a commandment, or misunderstood it, or unknowingly failed to fulfil it. This is a person who knows God's Word perfectly well and yet deliberately chooses to despise and reject it. God says that such a person "reproaches Yahweh," and that he "has despised the word of Yahweh and has broken His commandment." Therefore, instead of being treated like the unintentional offender, that person was to be cut off from among the people, and the guilt remained upon him (Numbers 15:30-31). The hand lifted high is the picture of open defiance, a fist raised against heaven, a person sinning boldly and on purpose, knowing full well what God has said and doing the opposite anyway.

The difference here is very important, and we must not miss it. Ignorance, once it was discovered, was to lead to correction, sacrifice, atonement, and forgiveness. But deliberate, defiant rebellion revealed a heart that knowingly despised God's authority. Yahweh graciously provided a way back for His people whenever they failed unknowingly, yet He would not allow deliberate rebellion to hide itself and pretend to be an innocent mistake. There is all the difference in the world between the person who stumbles in the dark and grieves when he sees his fault, and the person who sees the light clearly and tramples upon it with a lifted hand. The first finds mercy waiting for him.

The second has hardened his own heart against the very God who would have forgiven him. We, the New Creation, have a solemn and searching lesson to learn from this difference, and we will study that lesson in tomorrow's Morning Light.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, great and holy God, whose mercy is as vast as Your majesty,
We thank You that when Your people fail in ignorance, You provide a way back to Yourself.

You do not treat our unknowing faults as nothing, yet You cover them fully with atonement.

Keep us from ever lifting a defiant hand against the Word we know to be true.

Give us tender hearts that grieve at sin and quickly return to You, rather than hardened hearts.

Teach us to seek You sincerely, as Hezekiah's people sought You, and to receive Your healing.

"Great is Yahweh! He is most worthy of praise! His greatness is beyond discovery." - Psalm 145:3

In Christ name we pray. Amen.
